findings.claim: The proposed audit records cannot identify the version involved in a transition.

findings.claim: The implementation plan does not name the files that implement its migration, endpoints, authorization or feature flag.

uncertainties: R3's availability scope needs clarification: docs/design.md:15 says every node within 60 seconds, while accepted docs/adr-002-fail-static-serving.md:14-15 explicitly accepts that rollbacks cannot propagate during registry outages. That accepted continuity tradeoff is not itself a defect.

The supplied files do not establish the existing assignments table, polling scheduler, serving-client implementation or enforcement of the asserted 30-second fleet deadline (docs/design.md:38,45,61). Their absence here does not prove they do not exist elsewhere. Planned integration and convergence checks at lines 89-91 are not passed-test evidence.

Atomicity between the guarded assignment update and rollout_events insertion is unspecified (docs/design.md:26-28,72-73). If committed separately, a failure could leave a transition without its promised audit event.

Dual-version capacity and artifact mutability remain unspecified: artifacts exceed 20 GB (docs/adr-003-object-storage-artifacts.md:6), while docs/design.md:41-42 requires both versions loaded. A registration checksum check at lines 55-57 also needs an immutability or load-time verification assumption if objects can later change.

Serving-client access to the assignment endpoint is unspecified. docs/design.md:75-82 assigns every endpoint the mutation-capable registry:rollout role; if serving clients use that GET, their read authorization needs clarification. Whether flag disablement preserves operator rollback access for active canaries is also unspecified (lines 88,92-93).

findings.claim: The unconditional rollback bound conflicts with the accepted outage exception.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:15 promises every-node rollback within 60 seconds; lines 44–46 call 50 seconds the worst case. docs/adr-002-fail-static-serving.md:9–15 explicitly accepts unchanged assignments, including rollbacks, during outages. docs/design.md:50–51 and src/rollout.py:36–40 preserve cached assignments on connection failure.
findings.rationale: A node unable to fetch a committed rollback can keep routing its cached canary beyond 60 seconds. The documented guarantee and acceptance criterion therefore overstate the supported behavior. Qualify R3 and the calculation while preserving the accepted fail-static decision.

uncertainties: Backout intent: docs/design.md:88,92–93 disables all transition endpoints while retaining assignments; src/rollout.py:24–31 continues an active canary split. Clarify whether backout intentionally freezes traffic or requires clearing canaries or retaining rollback access. Ending active canaries during software backout is not an explicit requirement. The two-model pilot also needs a defined flag scope (docs/design.md:90).

Timing and measurement: docs/design.md:38–46,90–91 assumes one-poll propagation, but src/rollout.py:34–43 fetches models sequentially without a visible timeout or scheduling bound. Slow fetches could exceed the estimate; client behavior is unknown. Define the measurement origin, every-node observation and whether completion means assignment adoption or finished requests. Actual timing failure is unproven.

Loading readiness: docs/design.md:40–42 assumes both versions resident, while lines 55–57 establish checksum admission only. docs/adr-003-object-storage-artifacts.md:5–13 describes large downloads, and src/rollout.py:24–30,34–43 shows no loading gate. An external loader might ensure readiness before activation; unavailable-version routing is conditional on that contract being absent.

Audit scope: docs/design.md:72–73 omits version identity from events; lines 61–69,79–80 overwrite current version fields. The described records cannot reconstruct which version a historical transition concerned. Whether version-level reconstruction is required by 'for audit' remains unspecified.

Audit atomicity: docs/design.md:26–28,72–73 does not specify whether assignment updates and event inserts share a transaction. Separate commits could lose or misrepresent an event, but no supplied implementation demonstrates separate commits.

Read authorization: docs/design.md:75–82 groups assignment GET under registry:rollout; src/rollout.py:37 performs fleet reads. Serving credentials and server authorization are absent, so neither broken polling nor excessive transition privileges is established.

Transition choices: docs/design.md:25–28,55–57,77–81 leaves behavior for a second canary, promotion or rollback without a canary, and checksum-failure responses open. These require decisions before implementation; no particular error status or failing endpoint can be inferred.

Implementation detail: docs/design.md:61–73,86–89 omits event field types and constraints, existing-row treatment for updated_by, implementation file operations and backend integration locations. These are readiness gaps, not evidence of defective existing migrations or missing promised current code.

Verification remains planned: docs/design.md:88–91 specifies transition/409 tests and fleet trials without complete assertions for the stated percent, role, checksum, generation and audit controls. No supplied results establish that these checks passed, and none were executed here.

Documentation preferences: docs/design.md:21–93 contains no alternatives discussion, but this alone establishes no incorrect architecture. Exact heading choices and more precise wording for 'serving is unaffected' (lines 50–51) are editorial preferences. Object storage follows accepted ADR-003; superseded ADR-001 does not require restoring NFS.

findings.claim: The shared HTML cache exposes one recipient's private content to other recipients.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:31–33 keys complete rendered HTML only by locale and run_date and reuses it on hits. src/notifications.py:13–15 embeds the recipient's name and notification bodies. docs/design.md:40–41 marks each accepting job's own event IDs emailed.
findings.rationale: Recipients sharing a locale receive the first cached recipient's name and activity, violating docs/design.md:14. Their own captured events can also be marked emailed despite being absent from their email. Render personal content separately for each recipient and retain that job's prepared body for retries.

findings.claim: The prescribed single retrieval omits eligible notifications above 100 rows.

findings.claim: The production dispatch budget cannot meet the required 08:00 deadline.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:8–9 specifies 180,000 recipients, all with pending rows and valid addresses. Lines 46–48 permit only two workers at 1,000 provider requests per minute throughout the hour, with no other sender. src/notifications.py:18–23 submits one recipient message per request.
findings.rationale: The hourly ceiling is 120,000 requests, leaving at least 60,000 recipients undispatched at 08:00, contrary to docs/design.md:15. Ideal completion takes 90 minutes, until 08:30, before retries or rendering. Rendering-cache hits do not eliminate recipient-specific provider requests; increase dispatch capacity with retry headroom.

uncertainties: Address correction needs clarification: docs/design.md:44 permits correction before acceptance, while :39 and :60 require stored-address retries and immutable prepared payloads. Restricting correction to unprepared jobs could reconcile these rules.

Accepted ADR-002:9 establishes 30-day retention. No supplied evidence disproves the stated binding guarantee or establishes that planned fault injection passed.

If daily runs overlap unresolved retries, events still eligible under emailed_at IS NULL (src/notifications.py:7) could enter differently dated jobs (docs/design.md:27,36,65). The policy for repeated event inclusion across dates is unspecified.

Lease ownership checks after expiry are unspecified (docs/design.md:24–25); their absence from the description does not prove stale workers corrupt state. The supplied context also does not establish database-engine incompatibility with the proposed locking clause.

Rollback explains completion of prepared jobs but leaves queued and claimed jobs' disposition unclear (docs/design.md:59,76–77). Whether rollback pauses enrollment or replaces application code, and how retry observation spans the seven-day window, remain open details.

The advancement condition checks no queued jobs at 08:00 (docs/design.md:75), while :59 permits unfinished claimed/prepared jobs. It could pass without complete dispatch; clarify the intended completion assertion. Insufficient capacity proves unfinished jobs, not necessarily queued jobs.

Alternatives comparison and file-level implementation/checkpoint detail are absent from docs/design.md:19–65,68–70. These are documentation and planning gaps, not additional demonstrated behavior defects. Separate headings and replacing 'accepts' at :74 are presentation preferences. 'Rows are immutable' at :6 needs scoping alongside emailed_at updates at :40–41.

Fault injection, 250-row and full-launch exercises, and rollout gates at docs/design.md:71–75 are planned checks; no supplied results establish that they passed. Accepted ADR-001:6–12 specifies UTC scheduling, and ADR-002:6–9 specifies provider acceptance rather than mailbox delivery; neither local-time delivery nor bounce recovery is an unmet requirement.

findings.claim: The proposed HTML cache sends one recipient's private content to other recipients sharing a locale and run date.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:31-33 keys the cache by (locale, run_date), renders the first recipient's name and event bodies on a miss, and reuses that HTML on a hit. src/notifications.py:13-15 embeds the supplied name and event bodies directly in the HTML. docs/design.md:36 dispatches the resulting body to each job's captured address.
findings.rationale: The key omits recipient identity and content. After the first render, subsequent recipients with that locale receive the first recipient's name and notifications instead of their own. This violates the recipient-only disclosure requirement in docs/design.md:14 and also omits the later recipients' required content. The stated launch population spans only 12 locales (docs/design.md:8), so recipient sharing of cache keys is inherent in the proposed launch.

findings.claim: Calling the existing retrieval helper once truncates digests at 100 notifications.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:7 allows 250 pending rows per recipient, and docs/design.md:13 requires every pending row through cutoff without truncation. docs/design.md:27-29 calls pending_for_user once and treats its result as complete. src/notifications.py:8 applies LIMIT 100. docs/design.md:69 explicitly reuses the existing retrieval function.
findings.rationale: A recipient with 250 eligible rows gets only the oldest 100 captured and rendered; 150 eligible rows are absent from that day's digest. Marking only the captured IDs emailed (docs/design.md:40-41) leaves the omitted rows pending but does not satisfy the current digest's inclusion requirement.

findings.claim: The production worker budget cannot dispatch the stated launch batch within the required hour.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:8-9 specifies 180,000 enabled recipients, all with valid addresses and pending rows. docs/design.md:15 requires dispatch between 07:00 and 08:00 UTC. docs/design.md:46-48 permits two workers at 1,000 provider requests per minute each, with no other sender. ADR-002:6-7 defines completion as provider acceptance.
findings.rationale: Even with immediate successful acceptance and no rendering cost or retries, two workers can issue at most 120,000 requests in 60 minutes. Each nonempty recipient needs a dispatch, leaving at least 60,000 recipients unaccepted at 08:00. The minimum dispatch time is 90 minutes. Alerts cannot supply the missing capacity.

uncertainties: docs/design.md:71-75 describes future crash-recovery exercises, launch-batch checks, and rollout gates. The supplied sources provide no results demonstrating those checks have passed; end-to-end recovery and rollout readiness remain unverified.

findings.claim: The shared HTML cache sends one recipient's private content to other recipients in the same locale.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:31-33 keys the cache by (locale, run_date), renders the first recipient's name and event bodies, and reuses that HTML on subsequent hits. src/notifications.py:13-15 embeds the supplied user's name and event bodies in the returned HTML. docs/design.md:36 sends the body to each job's captured address.
findings.rationale: Recipients sharing a locale and date receive the first cached recipient's name and notifications instead of their own. This directly violates the recipient-only disclosure requirement in docs/design.md:14. Persisting each job's body preserves the incorrect content for retries. Recipient-specific rendered content must not be shared under this cache key.

findings.claim: Calling the existing retrieval helper once truncates eligible notification sets above 100 rows.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:7 allows 250 pending rows, and docs/design.md:13 requires every eligible row without truncation. docs/design.md:27-29 calls pending_for_user once and claims it returns the complete set. src/notifications.py:6-10 applies ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 100. docs/design.md:69 proposes reusing the existing retrieval function.
findings.rationale: A recipient with 250 eligible rows gets only the oldest 100 in this digest; 150 are absent from the stored IDs and rendered body. Those rows remain pending when only captured IDs are marked emailed (docs/design.md:40-41), but later processing does not satisfy inclusion in this cutoff's digest. The retrieval implementation or retrieval plan must change to obtain the complete set.

findings.claim: The production worker budget cannot dispatch the stated launch batch within the required hour.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:8-9 specifies 180,000 enabled launch recipients, all with valid addresses and pending rows. docs/design.md:15 requires dispatch between 07:00 and 08:00 UTC. docs/design.md:46-48 limits production to two workers, each capped at 1,000 provider requests per minute, with no other sender. docs/adr-002-dispatch-completion.md:6-7 defines completion as provider acceptance.
findings.rationale: Two workers can make at most 120,000 requests in 60 minutes. With one acceptance required per recipient, at least 60,000 recipients miss the window even with instant rendering and no retries or failures. The minimum dispatch time is 90 minutes. The 100% rollout therefore cannot meet its no-queued-jobs-at-08:00 gate (docs/design.md:73-75) under the stated budget.

uncertainties: docs/design.md:24-25, 34, 40-42, 68-71 leaves implementation choices unresolved: it names no migration, scheduler, or worker files and specifies neither lease renewal timing nor how an expired claimant is prevented from overwriting a successor's preparation. The safety of concurrent recovery depends on those choices. The crash and launch-batch exercises in docs/design.md:71-75 are planned requirements; successful results are not supplied.

docs/design.md:43-44 allows address correction before provider acceptance, while docs/design.md:60 makes prepared payloads immutable. The treatment of a prepared job that fails with an address error is unclear, including whether its captured address can change. Likewise, docs/design.md:76-77 does not say what happens to queued or claimed jobs during rollback, so completion of those jobs cannot be established.

docs/design.md:63 assumes an existing service credential, but README.md:1-3 and src/notifications.py:18-26 provide no credential setup or reference. Deployment authentication remains an unstated prerequisite; the supplied sources do not establish that it will fail. The stated provider idempotency contract in docs/design.md:37-38 is consistent with the accepted retention decision in docs/adr-002-dispatch-completion.md:9, but no provider integration evidence is supplied.

findings.claim: The proposed request contract permits a signed-in customer to export another customer's data to a chosen email address.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:38-42 requires a signed-in session but takes both user_id and delivery_email from the body, without specifying ownership or support-role authorization. Lines 63-65 send the resulting bearer link to that address. The existing customer path binds user_id to session.user_id (src/privacy_exports.py:8-17).

findings.claim: The proposed worker pool cannot sustain the required request volume.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:25-27 requires fulfillment within 72 hours and steady throughput of 1,200 requests/day. Lines 54-56 specify four serial workers and six minutes per export, claiming this covers R3.
findings.rationale: Even at continuous utilization, capacity is 4 × 1,440 / 6 = 960 exports/day. At 1,200 arrivals/day, backlog grows by at least 240 daily, eventually violating R2 as well as immediately failing R3. Retries and additional processing further reduce capacity. Five workers would only match average arrivals without headroom.

findings.claim: The rollout drops outstanding legacy requests without a migration or drain step.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:12-15 describes roughly 300 open export_tasks with deadlines. Lines 86-94 introduce export_requests and eventually drop export_tasks, but never transfer or finish its open rows. src/privacy_exports.py:11-17 stores request identity and deadlines there; lines 49-50 close those rows.

New request routing does not preserve previously submitted requests or their original deadlines. Retirement must explicitly account for the outstanding tasks.

findings.claim: Flag-only rollback cannot restore the legacy workflow after the final rollout step.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:90-94 moves settings traffic behind the flag, removes the console export action, and drops export_tasks. Lines 96-97 specify only disabling the flag as rollback. The legacy open_task and close_task functions require export_tasks (src/privacy_exports.py:8-18,49-50).

The previous intake/completion path therefore cannot function as the fallback implied by the rollout. A rollback boundary or a working replacement recovery procedure is missing.

uncertainties: docs/design.md:41-59,70-82 does not identify the queue service, durable enqueue mechanism, or recovery for interrupted jobs. Whether a committed request can lose its job, or a redelivered job can duplicate delivery, depends on implementation choices that remain unspecified.

docs/design.md:58-59,96-97 pages on-call after retry exhaustion and pauses queued work during rollback, but specifies no recovery procedure or maximum pause. Meeting the 72-hour requirement during these conditions is unresolved.

docs/design.md:66 attributes the seven-day retention maximum to a bucket lifecycle rule. The supplied sources do not establish the rule's deletion timing or treatment of retained object versions; whether it strictly satisfies R4 remains unverified.

docs/design.md:46-56 measures existing build_export, while the proposed job adds support tickets, compression, storage, and delivery. End-to-end runtime is unknown; the stated measurement does not validate full-pipeline capacity.

docs/design.md:86-92 proposes staff archive comparisons and queue monitoring; no results are supplied. API, worker, migration and configuration file locations, authorization tests, support-ticket coverage checks, failure recovery tests and load acceptance criteria remain unspecified. The existing build_export covers only profile, orders and addresses (src/privacy_exports.py:35-46), so comparison with legacy exports alone cannot establish support-ticket completeness. No planned check is treated as passed.

findings.claim: The specified request contract allows a signed-in customer to export another customer's data.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:38-42 requires a session but takes user_id and delivery_email from the caller. docs/design.md:63-65 emails the archive's bearer link to that address. The existing customer flow instead derives user_id from session.user_id (src/privacy_exports.py:8-17).

Customer identity must be bound to the session, with authorized support requests handled explicitly. This defect concerns request authorization; login-free downloads are accepted by docs/adr-001-presigned-download-links.md:12-19.

findings.rationale: The stated capacity is 4 × 1,440 / 6 = 960 exports/day at continuous utilization. At the forecast load, backlog grows by 240 requests/day even before retries or downtime. This directly fails R3 and eventually exceeds R2's 72-hour fulfillment target (docs/design.md:25-26). Five workers would only match average arrivals without headroom.

findings.claim: The cutover deletes legacy request storage and fulfillment without addressing the known backlog.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:14-15 identifies roughly 300 open tasks with existing deadlines. docs/design.md:86-94 provides no drain or migration before removing the console action and dropping export_tasks. src/privacy_exports.py:8-18 stores each request's subject, creation time and deadline there; src/privacy_exports.py:49-50 completes tasks through that table.
findings.rationale: Executing the written cutover discards outstanding request records and their original deadlines while removing their handling path. New export_requests do not preserve those obligations automatically. A defined completion or migration gate is needed before retirement.

uncertainties: docs/design.md:93-97: disabling the flag pauses accepted work and cannot recreate the retired table or console action. Post-retirement recovery is unspecified; a 72-hour breach depends on pause duration and recovery behavior.

docs/design.md:41-42,49-50,58-64: durable enqueue, duplicate-job handling, upload/status/email interruption recovery and exhausted-retry recovery are unspecified. Stranded requests or duplicate delivery are conditional implementation risks, not demonstrated failures.

docs/design.md:47-56 and src/privacy_exports.py:35-46: the historical six-minute measurement covers existing collectors and JSON generation, not demonstrated timing for added support tickets, compression, upload and notification. The capacity defect holds even accepting that measurement.

docs/design.md:88-92 proposes staff comparisons and metric observation; no completed results or acceptance thresholds are supplied. Legacy exports omit support tickets (src/privacy_exports.py:35-46), so comparison criteria must distinguish existing content from newly added content. Authorization, load, recovery, migration and rollback have not been established as validated.
docs/design.md:25-26,63-64 does not define whether fulfillment means archive readiness, email sending or successful delivery. The intended event affects measurement of R2.

docs/design.md:28,66 proposes lifecycle retention, but actual deletion timing and deployed configuration are unverified. Deployment of the bucket controls accepted in docs/adr-001-presigned-download-links.md:12-20 is also unestablished; their absence is not demonstrated.

docs/design.md:47-52: the supplied sources do not establish an exhaustive database inventory or support-ticket ownership/output contract. The risk-score exclusion is expressly accepted by docs/adr-002-exclude-risk-scores.md:10-18; qualifying R1's broad wording at docs/design.md:23-24 is a clarity preference, not a missing-data defect.

docs/design.md:34-97 lacks a complete implementation file map and detailed acceptance cases; intermediate worker behavior before the collector is added at docs/design.md:86-89 remains open. Additional planning detail, clickable ADR references and consolidated headings could improve handoff, but no particular template or additional architecture alternative is required by the supplied sources.

findings.claim: The proposed request handler permits a signed-in customer to request another customer's export.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:38-42 accepts user_id and delivery_email from the body, requires only a customer or support session, and uses that user_id to create the request. docs/design.md:63-65 sends the archive link to the supplied address without requiring login for download. The existing path binds the subject to session.user_id (src/privacy_exports.py:8-17).

Supporting agent submissions does not require allowing customers to select arbitrary subjects. Subject authorization must distinguish customer requests from authorized support submissions; the accepted bearer-link delivery decision does not authorize arbitrary request subjects.

findings.claim: The specified worker pool cannot sustain the required steady-state request volume.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:27 requires 1,200 requests/day. docs/design.md:54-56 specifies four workers, one export per worker at a time, averaging six minutes per export, and claims this covers R3. docs/design.md:25-26 requires fulfillment within 72 hours.

The queue cannot reach steady state, and waiting times eventually exceed 72 hours. This shortfall exists before allowing for retries or additional support-ticket collection.

findings.claim: The rollout drops the legacy request table without migrating or draining its open requests.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:11-15 describes roughly 300 open export_tasks with existing deadlines. src/privacy_exports.py:8-18 stores requests and due_at in that table. docs/design.md:40-42 and 82 route new requests through export_requests jobs. docs/design.md:86-94 switches entry points, removes the console export action and drops export_tasks, with no transfer or drain step.
findings.rationale: Open legacy requests have no described route into the automated queue. Dropping their table deletes their request records and deadlines while removing the manual fulfillment action. The rollout therefore leaves outstanding requests unfulfilled and loses the information needed to track their original deadlines. It needs an explicit migration or completion prerequisite before removing the legacy path.

uncertainties: docs/design.md:96-97 pauses queued requests until the flag is re-enabled. Whether rollback violates the 72-hour requirement depends on its duration and existing request ages; no maximum pause or alternate processing path is specified.

docs/design.md:40-42 describes inserting a request and enqueueing a job but does not specify atomicity or recovery. An interruption between those operations could strand a request if no durable handoff or reconciliation exists; the supplied sources do not establish that behavior.

docs/design.md:47-48 and 88-89 proposes a support-ticket collector and comparisons for 20 staff accounts. src/privacy_exports.py:35-46 currently includes only profile, orders and addresses. The proposed collector's correctness and archive comparison results are unavailable; the planned comparisons cannot establish completed validation.

docs/design.md:23-24 states broad coverage, while ADR-002:10-18 explicitly excludes risk_scores. This is a wording inconsistency, not a missing-data defect under the accepted decision. ADR-001:13-20 also explicitly accepts unauthenticated, object-scoped links lasting at most 72 hours and their bearer-access consequence, consistent with docs/design.md:63-65.

findings.claim: The payout computation ignores refunds and can pay sellers whose settled balance is below the accepted minimum.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:26-28 assumes record_refund() inserts negative rows and specifies SUM(amount_cents). src/ledger.py:28-32 instead increments refunded_cents on the existing order row. src/ledger.py:44-48 calculates settled balance as SUM(amount_cents - refunded_cents). docs/adr-001-weekly-payout-schedule.md:9-11 requires a settled balance of at least $25.00.
findings.rationale: For a settled $40 sale with a $20 refund, the proposed batch computes $40 although the ledger balance is $20. It would transfer $20 too much and bypass the $25 eligibility threshold. The batch must use the existing net-amount representation or explicitly migrate the ledger representation and its writers consistently.

findings.claim: The payout detail endpoint lacks a seller ownership check and exposes other sellers' payout details to authenticated callers.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:50-51 scopes the list endpoint to the JWT sub. In contrast, docs/design.md:51-54 says the detail handler loads by payout_id and returns the payout after the gateway verifies the JWT. docs/design.md:59-61 defines sequential BIGSERIAL payout IDs and a seller_id column.
findings.rationale: Authentication establishes the caller's identity but does not establish ownership of the requested payout. Supplying another seller's ID would return that seller's amount, status, destination account suffix and included orders. The detail lookup must also match seller_id to the authenticated seller.

uncertainties: docs/design.md:24-26 references HoldPolicy without defining its duration, reference time or source in the supplied files. Eligibility beyond the accepted settled-balance minimum cannot be determined; this is an unresolved policy detail, not evidence that a particular hold duration is wrong.

docs/design.md:38-46 correctly budgets 100 minutes for 90,000 initial transfer requests, consistent with docs/adr-002-paylane-transfers.md:6-9. That leaves capacity for 18,000 additional requests within two hours at the account limit. Pending replays, retries and other processing could exhaust that allowance, but their volumes and durations are unspecified, so a window overrun is conditional.

docs/design.md:35-38 makes payout insertion and ledger updates transactional but does not specify row locking or conditional claims. If overlapping executions select the same settled entries before either commits, separate payout IDs could produce duplicate transfers despite stable keys per payout. The sources do not establish whether overlapping execution is possible or serialized.

src/ledger.py:36-40 unconditionally sets an order's entries to settled. If fulfilment invokes settle() again after payout, it would make paid_out entries eligible again, conflicting with docs/design.md:15. Duplicate fulfilment invocation is not established by the supplied sources, so this remains a conditional risk.

docs/design.md:70-82 describes migration, sandbox comparison and two shadow runs as rollout acceptance gates. No supplied results establish that these gates have been completed or that the planned comparisons passed. Their future success cannot be used as evidence that the current computation is correct.

findings.claim: The payout calculation ignores refunds and can pay sellers below the accepted minimum.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:26-28 claims record_refund() inserts negative refund rows and sums amount_cents. src/ledger.py:28-33 instead increments refunded_cents on the existing order row; src/ledger.py:44-48 subtracts that field. docs/adr-001-weekly-payout-schedule.md:10 requires at least $25 settled balance.
findings.rationale: For an otherwise selected $30 sale refunded by $10, the existing balance is $20, but the proposed calculation pays $30. Use the existing net-balance representation or explicitly design its migration and refund-writer changes.

findings.claim: The detail endpoint omits seller ownership authorization.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:50 scopes the list to JWT sub, but docs/design.md:51-54 specifies loading detail by payout_id and returning it after session verification. docs/design.md:60-61 defines a sequential payout_id and a seller_id.
findings.rationale: Following the specified lookup lets an authenticated seller request another seller's payout identifier and receive its amount, orders, and bank-account suffix. Require the detail lookup to match the authenticated seller as well as payout_id.

findings.claim: The eligibility calculation depends on an undefined HoldPolicy.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:25-26 introduces an order hold window without defining its duration, timestamp, implementation, or reference. src/ledger.py:9-15 has no order timestamp; src/ledger.py:36-40 defines settlement after delivery. docs/adr-001-weekly-payout-schedule.md:9-11 defines eligibility using settled balance and the minimum.
findings.rationale: The supplied sources do not determine which settled entries to select. Implementing this proposal requires inventing an additional eligibility rule and its data source, so weekly payout amounts cannot be specified reproducibly.

findings.claim: No source or mapping is defined for the seller's destination account.
findings.evidence: README.md:3 requires bank transfers. docs/design.md:35-38 sends a payout through Paylane, and docs/design.md:51-52 promises the destination's last four digits. Neither the payout schema at docs/design.md:59-67 nor LedgerEntry at src/ledger.py:9-15 contains destination information; docs/adr-002-paylane-transfers.md:6 only identifies the sending merchant account.
findings.rationale: The defined records cannot determine where to send a seller's funds or provide the promised destination details. The design must identify the account source, seller mapping, and association with each payout.

findings.claim: The implementation plan omits required API and webhook work and leaves code locations undecided.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:72 names a migration and docs/design.md:74-78 specifies batch comparison and shadow runs. No step names implementation files or verification for the status-changing webhooks required at docs/design.md:41-43 or the endpoints required at docs/design.md:50-54.
findings.rationale: The stated completion gates can be satisfied without delivering payout status processing or seller access. The plan needs concrete changes and checks for these components before cutover; batch-total comparisons alone do not establish their behavior.

uncertainties: The 100-minute calculation is correct for 90,000 initial requests (docs/design.md:45-46). Pending replays and retries (docs/design.md:37-41) also consume the account's 15 requests/second allowance (docs/adr-002-paylane-transfers.md:7). Their volume and processing overhead are unstated, so completion within two hours is unverified, not demonstrably impossible.

Overlapping runs are unspecified. The transaction at docs/design.md:35-36 does not describe locking or conditional entry claims. If concurrent workers or restarts overlap, confirm that the same entries cannot fund distinct payout IDs; stable keys alone protect only retries of one payout.

If fulfilment repeats settlement after payout, src/ledger.py:36-40 unconditionally restores settled status, making those entries selectable again under docs/design.md:24-25. Repeated settlement is not established by the sources; clarify whether delivery processing prevents it or needs a state guard.

Signed final events are required by docs/adr-002-paylane-transfers.md:10, but authentication, event-to-payout mapping, and repeated or conflicting event handling are unspecified at docs/design.md:41-43. Delivery guarantees are not supplied, so resulting failure scenarios remain conditional.

Rollback resends pending payouts until terminal webhooks (docs/design.md:79-82), without explicitly preserving the 21-day cutoff and finance reconciliation rule at docs/design.md:38-41. Clarify how aged or missing-webhook payouts finish rollback. Resending beyond 30 days has no stated idempotency guarantee (docs/adr-002-paylane-transfers.md:8-9).

Staging comparisons and two shadow weeks are future completion gates (docs/design.md:72-78). No results are supplied; they cannot be counted as passed validation. The carried-balance dashboard behavior accepted at docs/adr-001-weekly-payout-schedule.md:14 also has no identified implementation or verification path.

findings.claim: Payout computation ignores refunds recorded by the existing ledger.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:26–28 claims refunds are negative rows and sums amount_cents. src/ledger.py:28–33 instead increments refunded_cents on the original row; src/ledger.py:44–48 calculates balances using amount_cents - refunded_cents. docs/design.md:59–67 proposes no refund-model conversion.
findings.rationale: A selected $100 sale refunded $30 contributes $100 instead of $70. Gross summation can also trigger a payout when the net balance is below the $25 minimum accepted in docs/adr-001-weekly-payout-schedule.md:9–11.

findings.claim: The specified payout detail lookup omits seller ownership authorization.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:50 scopes the list to JWT sub, but lines 51–54 describe authenticating the JWT and loading detail solely by payout_id. docs/design.md:60–61 models a sequential payout identifier and seller_id.
findings.rationale: As specified, an authenticated seller can retrieve another seller's payout amount, bank-account suffix and included orders. Authentication does not establish ownership; detail retrieval must enforce the authenticated seller boundary.

findings.claim: Failure erases the order membership promised for historical payout details.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:51–52 promises included orders. The sole modeled entry-to-payout association is ledger_entries.payout_id at line 67. Lines 41–43 explicitly clear it when a payout fails; lines 35–36 assign it when entries enter another payout.
findings.rationale: The failed payout remains in payouts, but its original orders can no longer be recovered from the modeled relationship. Retain historical membership independently of current reservation state to support the stated response.

uncertainties: docs/design.md:25–26 references an undefined HoldPolicy. Neither the supplied source nor accepted ADRs defines its duration or required timestamps. Eligibility and its relationship to the settled-balance rule in docs/adr-001-weekly-payout-schedule.md:9–11 remain open.

docs/design.md:45–46 correctly calculates 100 minutes for 90,000 first requests. The 15-request/s account limit (docs/adr-002-paylane-transfers.md:6–9) permits at most 108,000 requests in two hours. Retries and pending replays (docs/design.md:37–40), plus processing overhead, consume the remaining capacity. No workload evidence proves a missed or satisfied window.

docs/design.md:35–38 does not specify exclusive execution or guarded entry claims. Overlapping runs could create different payout IDs and provider keys for the same entries; neither overlap nor inadequate database isolation is established.

src/ledger.py:36–40 unconditionally sets entries to settled. A repeated fulfilment notification after payout could reopen paid entries, contrary to docs/design.md:15. Whether such notifications repeat is unspecified.

docs/design.md:79–82 says rollback resends until all pending payouts become terminal, while lines 38–41 stop automatic replay after 21 days and require finance reconciliation. The general cutoff may also govern rollback; clarify reconciliation and resumption of manual exports. Indefinite replay beyond the accepted 30-day key window is not established.

Signed final-status webhooks are already required by docs/adr-002-paylane-transfers.md:10. Verification, duplicate/reordered event handling, refunds after reservation, and destination-account sourcing are unspecified in docs/design.md:35–54; their omission does not prove an unsafe implementation.

The staging and shadow comparisons in docs/design.md:74–78 are planned acceptance criteria, with no supplied execution evidence. Friday manual exports (line 5) and Monday batches (line 24) need aligned comparison snapshots; differing cutoffs are not established.

docs/design.md:72–82 leaves file scope, API/webhook build phases and edge-case verification underspecified. These are readiness gaps; they do not establish those components will be omitted. Alternatives prose and section layout are completeness or presentation concerns, not faults in the accepted schedule/provider choices.

findings.claim: The unchanged ingest API does not establish the tenant identity that downstream billing is instructed to trust.
findings.evidence: The design claims payload tenant_id is overwritten from authentication. src/ingest_api.py:11-18 returns an authentication record, but src/ingest_api.py:21-23 only checks success. src/ingest_api.py:30-37 forwards the payload tenant_id unchanged as both event tenancy and partition key.
findings.rationale: A caller with a valid API key can submit another tenant's identifier and attribute usage to that tenant. The proposed trust boundary therefore permits incorrect tenant billing. Bind or validate tenancy against the authenticated principal at ingest and revise the unchanged-ingest assumption.

findings.claim: The stated consumer sizing does not cover the required peak throughput.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:18 requires 60,000 events/s. docs/design.md:35-38 specifies sixteen consumers at 3,000 events/s each, totaling 48,000 events/s.
findings.rationale: At the stated sustained performance, peak arrivals exceed processing by 12,000 events/s and accumulate backlog. The claim that this sizing covers R2 is inconsistent with its own figures. Increase demonstrated aggregate capacity; tenant distribution and database throughput also require validation.

findings.claim: One-hour deduplication retention cannot guarantee exactly-once billing across existing client retries.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:43-52 drops previously seen IDs but deletes that evidence after one hour. src/meter_client.py:17-24 preserves event IDs in the spool; src/meter_client.py:26-47 retains batches after unsuccessful requests and permits retries within its 24-hour expiry window. Rollups remain open for 48 hours after the hour ends (docs/design.md:56-57).
findings.rationale: Acceptance followed by a lost response leaves the batch available for retry. A retry after deduplication cleanup, while the rollup remains open, adds the same event again and violates R1 (docs/design.md:17). Database-before-offset commit ordering does not prevent this producer retry. Preserve uniqueness evidence across the supported redelivery horizon.

uncertainties: Accepted ADR-001 already requires next-invoice billing of unbilled adjustments and setting billed_in (docs/adr-001-event-time-windows.md:12-17). Clarify the closed-rollups-only wording (docs/design.md:20,56-58); it does not establish removal of adjustment billing.

Accepted ADR-002 supplies tenant/date partitioning and deletion 400 days after creation (docs/adr-002-raw-event-archive.md:10-12); this is not a thirteen-month retention shortfall. Archive upload/offset/retry ordering and Kafka retention remain unspecified (docs/design.md:62-63), so recovery guarantees cannot be established, but event loss is not demonstrated.

First-row creation and coordination with closure are unspecified (docs/design.md:45-49,56-58,73-80). Locking existing rows alone does not explain initialization; an implemented race or loss is not established.
Initial offsets, historical billing ownership, tenant cutover and rollback are unspecified (docs/design.md:94-99). Overlapping or omitted billing depends on those choices.

The planned 0.1% comparison alone cannot demonstrate exactly-once correctness and can conceal offsetting errors (docs/design.md:17,95-98). Comparison interval, meter dimensions, denominator, zero totals and separate correctness gates need clarification. Neither the shadow cycle nor matching totals are established as completed.
R3's hour boundary and the customer-serving path for open rollups are unclear (docs/design.md:19,56-58). The supplied sources do not establish that an existing reader cannot satisfy it.

The asserted consumer benchmark was not independently validated; tenant skew, database capacity and maximum replay horizon are unknown (docs/design.md:35-38,51-52). A hot-tenant bottleneck depends on traffic distribution.

Ingest validates presence and negative quantity but not timestamp usability (src/ingest_api.py:32-37). Normalization and handling of accepted events incompatible with hourly aggregation remain undefined (docs/design.md:43-49,67-89); malformed production traffic is not established.

Alternatives, explicit risks and an executable implementation plan are absent from docs/design.md:25-99. These are document-completeness limitations; exact headings and template layout are preferences, not additional runtime defects. No planned validation is assumed passed.

findings.claim: The asserted tenant isolation does not exist in the unchanged ingest API.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:29-31 says authentication resolves the tenant and overwrites the payload tenant_id. authenticate() returns a record (src/ingest_api.py:11-18), but handle_ingest only checks whether it is None (22-23) and publishes using the unchanged event['tenant_id'] (36-37).
findings.rationale: A valid API key for tenant A can submit an event naming tenant B; ingest accepts it and publishes it under B's key. Downstream aggregation therefore attributes that usage to B, contradicting the design's trust assumption and corrupting tenant billing.

findings.claim: The proposed consumer capacity is below the required peak throughput.
findings.evidence: R2 requires 60,000 events/s (docs/design.md:18). The proposal specifies 16 partitions, one consumer per partition, and 3,000 events/s per consumer (35-38).
findings.rationale: The stated capacity totals 48,000 events/s, leaving a 12,000 events/s deficit at the required peak even with evenly distributed traffic. The supplied sizing therefore does not cover R2; processing at the stated per-consumer rate accumulates backlog during peak traffic.

findings.claim: Deduplication records expire while the client can still retry the same accepted event.
findings.evidence: The aggregator drops duplicates using seen_events but deletes records older than one hour (docs/design.md:43-52). The client retains its original batch after a request exception and expires failed events only after 24 hours (src/meter_client.py:8,26-47). R1 requires exactly-once billing (docs/design.md:17).
findings.rationale: If ingest accepts a batch but its response is lost, the client retains it. After the first aggregation and deletion of its deduplication record, a retry more than one hour later is treated as new. For an hour still open within the 48-hour window, its quantity is added again, double billing an accepted event.

findings.claim: Ingest accepts events with timestamps that cannot identify an event-time hour.
findings.evidence: src/ingest_api.py:32-35 checks field presence and nonnegative quantity, without validating timestamp. An otherwise valid event with timestamp='not-a-time' is published and receives 202 with accepted=1 (36-41). ADR-001:10-11 requires rollups keyed by event timestamp.
findings.rationale: An accepted event with no interpretable event time cannot be assigned its required hourly rollup. The unchanged ingest path admits data for which both event-time billing and counting every accepted event as specified (docs/design.md:17) cannot be satisfied; rejecting it downstream would still leave an accepted event uncounted.

uncertainties: Late adjustments have an explicit billing path: ADR-001:12-14 directs the billing service to read unbilled adjustments on the next invoice and set billed_in. The closed-rollup exporter in docs/design.md:54-58 does not establish that adjustments are omitted. How adjustment billing and marking remain atomic is unspecified.

Archive acknowledgement, offset handling, recovery, and Kafka retention are unspecified (docs/design.md:60-63); producer.send/flush durability also depends on the unavailable producer implementation (src/ingest_api.py:5,37-40). Loss of accepted events cannot be established from those omissions alone.

The handling of initially absent rollup rows and coordination between row creation, updates, and closure is not detailed (docs/design.md:45-49,56-57,73-79). A closure race depends on those implementation choices and is not demonstrated.

Tenant-key skew could further reduce usable throughput, but no tenant traffic distribution is supplied (docs/design.md:35-38). R3 feasibility beyond the demonstrated capacity shortfall remains unverified.
The shadow cycle and reconciliation are future rollout steps, with no supplied results. Their 0.1% acceptance tolerance alone cannot establish exactly-once billing (docs/design.md:17,92-99).

findings.claim: The claim that ingest replaces the payload tenant with the authenticated tenant is false.
findings.evidence: src/ingest_api.py:11-18 returns the API-key record, but :21-23 only checks whether authentication succeeds. Lines 30-37 retain the supplied tenant_id and publish it as both the event tenant and Kafka key. src/meter_client.py:12-20 also accepts tenant_id independently of api_key.
findings.rationale: A caller with a valid key can submit usage for another tenant. Keeping ingest unchanged preserves this attribution vulnerability while downstream billing explicitly trusts that field. Bind the tenant to the authenticated identity or enforce its authorized tenant scope before publishing.

findings.claim: The proposed consumer capacity does not cover the stated peak requirement.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:18 requires 60,000 events/s. Lines 35-38 specify 16 partitions, one consumer per partition, and 3,000 events/s per consumer: 48,000 events/s in total.
findings.rationale: Even accepting the stated consumer rate and assuming evenly distributed traffic, capacity falls short by 12,000 events/s at peak. Sustained peak traffic accumulates backlog, violating R2 and eventually delaying hourly visibility. Revise the partition/consumer capacity before claiming coverage.

findings.claim: Deleting deduplication records after one hour permits accepted retries to be billed twice.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:43-49 deduplicates through seen_events before incrementing usage_hourly; :51-52 deletes records older than one hour. src/meter_client.py:19 generates the ID when recording, :26-43 retains a batch after a request exception, and :8,45-47 permits retries until the event is 24 hours old. docs/adr-001-event-time-windows.md:10-11 keeps rollups open for 48 hours after the hour ends.
findings.rationale: If ingest accepts an event but its response is lost, the client can resend the same ID two hours later. After cleanup removes its seen_events record, the aggregator adds its quantity to the still-open rollup again. Transactional writes and subsequent Kafka offset commits do not prevent this later duplicate, contradicting R1. Deduplication must cover supported retries and any allowed replay.

uncertainties: docs/design.md:11-13 describes a nightly job and its six-hour runtime; :37-38 asserts load-test throughput. No job implementation, measurements, or test results are supplied. These claims remain unverified; the planned shadow comparison at :95-98 is not evidence of a completed check.

docs/design.md:19,40-49 gives a visibility deadline and database flush interval but identifies no customer read path. Files and concrete implementation steps for the aggregator, scheduler, archiver, schema deployment, and exporter are absent from :92-99. No executable acceptance tests or rollback procedure are specified, so implementation readiness and working rollout phases remain unresolved. The 0.1% comparison alone does not establish exactly-once behavior.

docs/adr-001-event-time-windows.md:12-14 already defines billing unbilled adjustments on the next invoice and setting billed_in. This remains authoritative alongside docs/design.md:56-58; omission of that explanation is not evidence that adjustments are discarded. Export retry behavior and atomic invoice assignment are not described, so duplicate-export risk cannot be resolved from these sources.

docs/design.md:62-63 and docs/adr-002-raw-event-archive.md:10-12 establish a second consumer and 400-day object retention. Kafka retention, archive write/offset ordering, recovery from partial writes, tenant/date partitioning in the implementation, and access controls are unspecified. Complete recoverable archival during failures therefore remains unestablished. The retention duration itself follows the accepted decision.

docs/design.md:35-52 provides no tenant-skew distribution, Postgres capacity evidence, consumer recovery details, or database availability plan. Tenant keying bounds a single tenant to one partition. Whether a hot tenant or database outage defeats the service targets depends on operational facts not supplied.

src/ingest_api.py:30-40 checks field presence and negative quantity but does not validate timestamp format. The aggregator's handling of accepted malformed timestamps is unspecified. Producer acknowledgment guarantees also depend on the unavailable metering.kafka implementation imported at :5. Neither successful durable acceptance nor poison-event recovery can be established from the supplied code.

findings.claim: The rollout leaves required implementation decisions unresolved.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:45-52 introduces snapshot_log, a chart response/UI contract and snapctl publish. Lines 55-63 describe creating/backfilling the log, replacing cron, enabling caching and shipping the UI, but identify no migration, job, command, API or UI implementation files and no step implementing snapctl. The supplied implementations are SnapshotReader.run (src/snapshot_reader.py:13-27) and ChartCache/cache_key (src/cache.py:11-25).
findings.rationale: An implementer must still choose the locations and integration contracts for the new components, including the rollback command required by R4 (docs/design.md:14,65-67). The rollout supplies acceptance milestones but not concrete implementation steps for all required behavior. This is an implementation-plan gap; it does not establish that the proposed runtime behavior is incorrect.

uncertainties: The proposed flow is understandable: build and validate a dated analytics schema under a job lock, publish a pointer, retain 14 snapshots, and serve tenant-scoped results through schema-specific cache keys. The current reader resolves the pointer once, sets a transaction-local search_path and supplies tenant_id as a query parameter (src/snapshot_reader.py:13-27). Cache misses use the schema actually returned, so the two pointer reads do not by themselves demonstrate incorrect cache placement (docs/design.md:34-42).

ADR-003:3,9-16 supersedes primary-querying ADR-001 and supports the analytics snapshot/failure fallback direction. ADR-002:6-14 explicitly delegates authentication to the gateway. Omitting service token verification is consistent with that decision. Gateway-only reachability and actual tenant SQL predicates cannot be verified: API/network configuration and chart SQL are absent; supplying tenant_id does not itself add a WHERE predicate (src/snapshot_reader.py:24-26).

The cron script, reporting-table inventory and consistent-export interface are not supplied. Thus docs/design.md:7-8's description of cron cannot be independently confirmed. The row-count publication gate also leaves the expected counts and comparison scope unspecified (docs/design.md:20-24,46-48); clarify whether both counts describe the same export before implementing it.

The 06:00 cutoff states intended behavior but does not explain cancellation of a stalled copy, coordination with publication, or recovery after process death (docs/design.md:19-25). A late publication would be a conditional failure, not an observed defect. The 28 h 59 min calculation is correct for consecutive daily snapshots; earlier failed nights can leave older data, which R3 explicitly accommodates (docs/design.md:11-13,28-29).

Schema cleanup and manual pointer changes need concurrency details if requests or rollback operations overlap retention. The reader does not explicitly pin a schema against deletion between pointer resolution and its query (src/snapshot_reader.py:15-26; docs/design.md:20,26,51-52,65-67). No such overlap or resulting failure is established by the supplied sources.

Cache failure policy is unspecified. ChartCache.get/put directly call Redis and propagate failures (src/cache.py:20-25); docs/design.md:34-40 does not say whether serving bypasses cache failures. Availability impact depends on the integration chosen. Redis deployment, access and capacity are also unspecified.

The seven successful nights, 50 requests/s latency test and forced-abandonment exercise are planned milestones, with no results supplied (docs/design.md:57-63). R2 and R4 are therefore unverified, not demonstrated failures. The 14-snapshot retention limit has no stated rationale or storage budget (docs/design.md:26,67); whether it is excessive or insufficient cannot be determined.

docs/design.md:19–25,46–52 does not define atomic pointer/log transitions, deadline cancellation or prevention of late publication. If those operations diverge after interruption, cleanup could delete a live schema. The publication interface also describes published targets while the job must first publish a new run. These are unresolved protocol questions; no faulty implementation is supplied.

docs/design.md:25–26,51–52,65–67 leaves older publication targets and coordination with retention unspecified. src/snapshot_reader.py:15–26 selects the pointer before accessing chart tables. If an older selected schema is deleted between those operations, a request can fail. The documented immediate-previous rollback remains within the 14-schema window; arbitrary-oldest rollback is not an established requirement.

docs/design.md:28–29 correctly computes 28 h 59 min assuming the preceding night succeeded. After a failed night, retained data can exceed 30 hours before recovery publication, as permitted by docs/adr-003-nightly-snapshots.md:16. Clarify whether R1 at docs/design.md:11 applies after publication or throughout a day whose job eventually succeeds.

docs/design.md:34–37,59–61 leaves cache-error handling, flag configuration and tenant-cohort selection undecided. src/cache.py:20–25 propagates Redis and decoding failures. Direct integration could reject a request despite available snapshot data, but that integration is not supplied. The cached representation and projection from the reader's schema/taken_at/rows result to the chart response also need definition (src/snapshot_reader.py:27; docs/design.md:49–50).

docs/design.md:57–63 describes future acceptance checks; no results establish successful publication, R2 latency or failed-run behavior. Cache warmth, tenant/chart/parameter diversity and publication transitions affect what a load test demonstrates. Specific lifecycle-race, interruption, tenant-isolation and five-minute rollback assertions remain unspecified (docs/design.md:11–14,65–67). No planned test is treated as passed.

docs/design.md:19–24,44–63 leaves reporting-table inventory, export mechanics, count-comparison baseline, advisory-lock identity/lifetime, log types/constraints, backfill metadata and implementation file scope open. These limit implementation readiness rather than prove incorrect behavior. In particular, the source export must define what fixed 01:00 taken_at represents for the displayed age (docs/design.md:22,49–50).

docs/design.md:21–22,39–40,46 does not define same-day execution after successful publication. If a retry rebuilt an existing published schema, schema-based cache keys could represent changed contents. Neither successful-run retries nor mutation of published schemas is required or established by the sources.

docs/adr-002-gateway-tenant-scoping.md:9–14 requires tenant scoping in every query and cache key. src/snapshot_reader.py:13–26 supplies tenant_id but accepts arbitrary SQL, so supplied parameters alone do not establish a tenant predicate. Actual chart SQL and deployment reachability are unavailable; no tenant leak or gateway bypass is demonstrated. Gateway token verification is the accepted architecture.

docs/design.md:1–67 has no separate detailed implementation plan or alternatives evaluation for its new mechanisms. Those are documentation/readiness limitations, not demonstrated product defects. Optional risk headings and consistent formatting of source paths at docs/design.md:6 are presentation preferences. Accepted snapshot serving and gateway authentication need not be reconsidered.

Performance and rollout validation remain unproven. docs/design.md:57-63 describes future completion criteria: seven timely nightly publications, a staging test at 50 requests/s meeting the p95 target, and a forced abandoned run preserving data and displaying age. No results are supplied. These are pending validations, not demonstrated failures or completed checks.

Tenant isolation depends on query text and deployment configuration absent from the supplied sources. src/snapshot_reader.py:24-26 supplies a tenant_id parameter but executes caller-provided SQL; supplying the parameter alone does not establish that SQL filters by tenant. ADR-002 requires tenant_id in every query and cache key (docs/adr-002-gateway-tenant-scoping.md:10-11), and gateway-only reachability (line 14). The cache key includes tenant_id (src/cache.py:11-13), and trusting the gateway header follows the accepted decision. Without actual chart SQL or deployment configuration, neither an unscoped query nor a gateway bypass is established.

Publication and log-state coordination need clarification. docs/design.md:19-26 makes running/abandoned schemas eligible for deletion, while publication updates the pointer; lines 46-52 define log states and a publication command accepting published schemas that the job also uses. The document does not specify the new schema's transition to published or whether that transition commits atomically with the pointer update. If the pointer could commit while the log still says running, a later job could delete the live schema, interrupting serving and failed-run fallback. A coordinated transition would avoid this; the supplied design does not establish that the unsafe state occurs.

findings.claim: Redemption does not enforce the token's purpose, allowing a reset token to authorize email verification.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:11 requires links to authorize only their respective operations. Lines 31-33 specify digest lookup and rejection for missing, consumed, or expired tokens; line 34 selects the operation solely from the HTTP route. Line 37 sets email_verified_at without checking purpose. Lines 53-55 store purpose but use it only to select the issuance template and expiry.
findings.rationale: Submitting a valid, unconsumed reset token to POST /email-verification satisfies all specified verification checks and marks an unverified account as verified. This directly violates operation isolation. Redemption must require the stored purpose to match the route before applying the account change.

findings.claim: Fixed mail capacity cannot satisfy the required issuance load and 60-second send-start deadline.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:13-14 requires 30 eligible requests per second for 10 minutes and sending to begin within 60 seconds of each accepted request. Line 43 creates one job per eligible request. Lines 44-45 fix capacity at two workers, each starting at most 10 sends per second. Line 48 excludes alternative sending paths and provider failures from this capacity scenario.
findings.rationale: The required profile creates 18,000 jobs in 600 seconds, while workers can start only 12,000 sends during that interval. Even with another 60 seconds, total capacity is only 13,200 starts, although every request's deadline has then elapsed. At least 4,800 jobs necessarily miss their deadlines even without failures. Capacity must increase or the requirements must be explicitly revised.

findings.claim: The proposed verification expiry contradicts the accepted 24-hour lifetime.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:23 gives verification tokens a 60-minute lifetime; lines 33 and 62 reject expired tokens and delete outbox jobs when links expire. docs/adr-001-link-lifetimes.md:3 marks the decision Accepted, and lines 7-8 require verification links to last 24 hours at every rollout stage. Line 12 identifies next-morning onboarding as the rationale.
findings.rationale: The proposed flow rejects verification links during the remaining 23 hours of their required validity window, including next-morning use. Pending verification mail also becomes eligible for deletion after only one hour. The design must use the accepted 24-hour verification lifetime.

uncertainties: docs/design.md:68 and 77-79 prescribe staging, load, concurrent-redemption, and session-invalidation checks, but no results are supplied. Their success is unverified. The session approach itself is consistent with docs/adr-002-sessions-and-mail.md:6-7 and src/accounts.py:10-28, which compare session versions and increment the account version on password updates.

docs/design.md:24-26 specifies equal HTTP responses but different persistence work for known and unknown accounts. Whether response timing reveals account existence under the requirement at line 15 remains unresolved; no timing behavior or measurements are supplied. This is a conditional disclosure risk, not an established leak.

findings.claim: Redemption does not enforce the token's purpose, allowing a reset token to verify an email address.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:11 requires operation isolation. Lines 31-34 look up a token by digest, reject only absent, consumed, or expired rows, and select the operation solely from the HTTP route. Lines 37-38 then permit verification and consumption. Lines 53-55 define purpose but use it only for issuance template and expiry.
findings.rationale: Submitting an unconsumed, unexpired reset token to POST /email-verification passes the stated checks and sets email_verified_at. The reset credential thereby authorizes a different operation and is consumed without resetting the password. Validate purpose against the route before applying either operation.

findings.claim: The fixed mail capacity cannot satisfy the required sending deadline at the required issuance rate.

findings.claim: The unconditional promise that connection loss aborts publication and database failures leave state unchanged cannot be guaranteed by the described transaction.

findings.claim: The proposed v1 money encoding violates the accepted checkout contract.

findings.claim: The proposed eligibility path accepts expired coupons.

findings.claim: Rounding tax once on the merchandise sum produces incorrect quotes under the required per-line rule.

The proposed aggregate call rounds 1 cent to 1 cent, understating tax and total by 1 cent. Tax differences can also go in the other direction. Sum individually rounded line taxes; the worked example at docs/design.md:58-60 does not expose this discrepancy because its line taxes are whole cents.

uncertainties: Performance remains unverified. docs/design.md:10 specifies p95 below 150 ms at 100 requests/s for up to 40 lines; lines 64-69 describe future checks and rollout gates, not measured results. The supplied sources establish no passing load-test result.

findings.claim: The proposed eligibility check accepts expired coupons, violating G5.

Lines 30-32 explicitly retrieve expired coupons and delegate eligibility to discount_cents, translating ValueError to 422. src/pricing.py:14-20 only checks the minimum subtotal before calculating the discount; it never reads expires_at. docs/design.md:21 incorrectly describes the existing helper as rejecting expired coupons. README.md:2 and docs/design.md:4 place eligibility validation in the trusted worker today.

A coupon with expires_at set to 2000-01-01, percent 10 and minimum 1,000 returns a 100-cent discount on a 1,000-cent subtotal without raising an exception. The specified route therefore persists an expired discount instead of returning 422. Add explicit expiry validation before applying the coupon and correct the description of existing behavior.

findings.claim: Aggregating merchandise before rounding tax violates the required per-line calculation and changes existing results.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:13 requires half-up rounding separately for each discounted line followed by summation. Lines 36-38 instead sum discounted merchandise and call tax_cents once. src/pricing.py:23-24 rounds each supplied amount, while src/pricing.py:27-29 currently invokes it separately for each line.
findings.rationale: For two discounted lines of 5 cents each at a 10% rate, existing and required tax is 1 + 1 = 2 cents. The proposed aggregate calculation returns 1 cent, reducing the stored tax and total incorrectly. The worked example at docs/design.md:58-60 produces equal results under both calculations and cannot expose this difference. Sum tax_cents over the allocated line nets, as internal_quote already does.

findings.claim: Returning decimal money strings from the new v1 route breaks the accepted checkout response contract.

A checkout string-rendering change does not satisfy the accepted endpoint versioning decision. Keep integer cents on this v1 route or explicitly revise the proposal to the coordinated v2 release specified by ADR-001.

uncertainties: docs/design.md:63-72 names implementation activities, tests and rollout gates, but leaves target files, the concrete quote schema/migration and stable error-code values unspecified. These implementation choices remain open; the supplied sources do not establish their intended values.

docs/design.md:27-29,40-42 requires cart locking for quote writers but does not describe how cart-content and address writers participate or advance cart revisions. If those writers bypass the same synchronization, a quote could commit against outdated cart contents; their implementation is not supplied.

The supplied src/pricing.py:27-35 defines arithmetic and a returned dictionary, not worker storage access. Worker compatibility with the new quote schema and rollout controls cannot be established from these sources.

findings.claim: The proposed v1 decimal-string response violates the accepted money contract and breaks checkout decoding.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:25 selects /v1; lines 52–53 encode money as decimal strings, and line 66 directs checkout to render them. Accepted docs/adr-001-v1-money.md:3–11 requires integer USD cents for all v1 pricing responses, explicitly includes recalculation, and states that checkout rejects strings. Decimal strings require a coordinated v2 release.

findings.claim: The specified eligibility path accepts expired coupons instead of returning HTTP 422.

Lines 21 and 32 claim and rely on expiry validation by discount_cents, while line 31 explicitly allows expired coupons through repository lookup. src/pricing.py:14–20 checks only minimum spend and calculates the discount; it never examines expires_at. findings.claim: Rounding tax once on aggregate merchandise violates G4 and changes tax and quote totals.

Two 5-cent lines at 10%, without a coupon, yield 2 cents under G4 versus 1 cent under the proposal.

uncertainties: docs/design.md:16,27–29,40–46 specifies shared locking for quote writers but does not establish how line, address and shipping mutations participate in locking and revision updates, or how checkout checks quote revisions. findings.claim: The backfill can overwrite a current dual-written value with a stale conversion.

findings.claim: The documented default throughput cannot meet the six-hour backfill requirement.

findings.claim: Contract execution in the same deploy breaks the accepted release sequencing and rollback guarantee.

findings.claim: The stated backfill defaults cannot meet the six-hour completion requirement.

findings.claim: The backfill can overwrite a newer dual-written target with a stale computed value.

uncertainties: docs/design.md:42 pauses above ten seconds of replica lag using five-second samples, but supplies no bound on lag growth between samples or outstanding replay work. docs/design.md:23-26 and 36-40 bound statement execution but provide no bound on commit latency while locks remain held. R1's two-second limit is therefore unproven under slow commits or lock contention; no actual violation is demonstrated by the supplied material.

src/runner.py:18-25 extracts an index name by splitting SQL and compares that token directly with pg_class.relname. src/runner.py:28-44 implements the existing runner, without the proposed phase dispatch, backfill worker, or timeout setup. docs/design.md:65-68 schedules that implementation and a staging run. findings.claim: Contract runs too early to preserve the accepted application rollback guarantee.
findings.evidence: docs/design.md:28-29 ships code that writes both columns; lines 48-51 drop the old columns immediately after backfill in the same deploy. docs/adr-002-expand-contract-releases.md:5-11 requires contract in a later release than the code that stopped using those columns, after that release has spent seven days in production. docs/design.md:13 repeats the rollback requirement.
